title: I Followed the Community-Risograph Hours Into the Drum They Left Inked

parts.text: I loaded drum A at 11:08 a.m. and intern Faye was already printing on my numbered masters. The screen said: ONE DRUM. NINETY MINUTES. INK STAYS WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-one, print co-op member, holding a job ticket that listed our color. Faye shrugged. "Interns are the drum." I photographed the screen, the ticket, and her copies on my stack. Then I asked for the riso log. At 11:16 the shop pinged why Faye's name was on my masters. I kept my voice shop-quiet and let the timestamp talk. A screen is only a screen until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The shop can see Faye's copies on my stack during our booking.

social.video_title: She printed on my numbered masters and left the drum inked — Part 1/2
social.description: Risograph, an intern on my stack, a ninety-minute screen she posted. I logged the copies. Would you have asked for the riso log?

parts.text: Faye called it a proof until the shop asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the screen, and the copies still. The drum went back to my rest. Faye ran her own ninety and told the next intern atmosphere was always about grain. Grain is a word interns use when a booking exists. Drum policy now has a second line: INTERNS ARE NOT THE DRUM. I keep our masters on a labeled hook. Faye brown-bags her jokes. The shop finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Interns are not the drum — Part 2/2
social.description: Riso log, numbered masters, and a second line on the screen. Was a proof ever my stack?
